title: TCS Will Give 50,000 Employees Access to Anthropic's AI. Its Chairman Wants Equal Numbers of Workers and AI Agents.
excerpt: India's largest IT company just struck a global deal with the maker of Claude — the same technology that helped wipe $63 billion off the sector in February
body:
India's largest IT services exporter has placed what may be its biggest bet yet on the technology that threatens to upend its own business model. Tata Consultancy Services announced a global strategic partnership with Anthropic on Thursday, becoming a Global Premier Partner in the Claude Partner Network and committing to equip 50,000 employees with the AI company's Claude models.

The scale of the deployment is staggering. TCS will roll out Claude access across engineering, finance, legal, marketing, and sales functions — not as a pilot, not as an experiment, but as enterprise-wide licensing. A dedicated Claude-focused AI business unit will develop solutions and deliver AI expertise with early access to new model releases. The partnership will target highly regulated sectors including financial services, healthcare, aviation, telecom, and public services.

## The Subtext Is Impossible to Miss

TCS Chairman N. Chandrasekaran said at the company's annual general meeting this week that TCS expects to move towards having an equal number of employees and AI agents in its workforce. The company cut more than 12,000 jobs last July, and headcount fell by more than 23,000 on a net basis in the fiscal year ended March 2026.

These are not abstract numbers. They represent a fundamental transformation of an industry that has been the single largest employer of Indian engineering graduates for two decades — and the primary vehicle for hundreds of thousands of NRIs to build careers in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Europe.

"Enterprise AI value comes from understanding business context, orchestrating complex systems, and applying deep AI engineering talent," TCS CEO K. Krithivasan said, framing the move as an opportunity rather than a retreat.

## Anthropic's India Play

For Anthropic, the deal deepens its commitment to what it calls its second-largest market. The San Francisco-based AI company has opened an office in India over the past year, hired for leadership roles, and expanded ties with multiple IT services firms. Rival Infosys struck a similar partnership with Anthropic in February, while OpenAI has roped in both Infosys and HCLTech.

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei noted the partnership's significance for India specifically. TCS's UK-based life and pensions business Diligenta, which serves over 22 million customers, plans to use Claude for customer service and process automation. TCS iON, the company's digital learning platform, will offer training and certification on Anthropic's models.

## What NRIs Should Watch

The Indian IT sector has lost more than $62.8 billion in market capitalisation since February, when Anthropic's launch of an AI agent tool spooked investors. TCS shares have fallen roughly 34 per cent this year. Infosys is down 31 per cent.

The question for the hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin workers in global IT is no longer whether AI will change their industry. It is whether the companies that built their careers can pivot fast enough to remain relevant — and whether the workers themselves can make the transition from writing code to orchestrating AI agents.

TCS is betting that its 600,000-strong workforce is an asset, not a liability, in this transition — a massive testing ground for AI deployment whose insights can then be replicated for clients. Whether that bet pays off will determine not just the future of India's most valuable IT company, but the career trajectories of an entire generation of Indian technologists working abroad.

The partnership becomes effective immediately. TCS will contribute capabilities to Anthropic's Claude Code ecosystem, including tools for claims adjudication and lending advisory — the kind of domain-specific work that has been the bread and butter of Indian IT for decades, now being rebuilt with AI at its core.

Sources: Reuters, TechCrunch, Verdict, The Hindu BusinessLine, Outlook Business
